original.text: I offer a concise, intentionally disquieting argument about why any putative scientific Theory of Everything (**TOE**) is epistemically constrained. The claim is simple and paradoxical: a TOE formulated within the conceptual and methodological bounds of human science can only be a theory of what our instruments, languages, and logics permit it to be. True totality — an account that includes itself and that which transcends its axioms — requires forms of self-description and meta-ontological operations that lie outside the epistemic reach of contemporary science. The result is that a TOE is, in practice, a "theory of most things," not of everything. I conclude with a dark irony: the most honest TOE may be the problem itself.

True totality — an account that includes itself and everything beyond its own axioms — needs forms of self-description and meta-level operations that sit outside the reach of contemporary science. So in practice a TOE ends up a "theory of most things," not of everything. And the conclusion is a dark irony: the most honest TOE may be the problem itself.

original.text:
[!info] Genre declaration
The logic employed here is held to ordinary standards of argument; the target — the idea of a Theory of Everything — is real and taken seriously. What follows is a *critique*: an epistemological argument about the limits of closed explanatory systems, not a result derivable from physics or mathematics. Where the prose turns poetic or ironic, that is deliberate — the theory of theories of everything is offered as creative metaphysics, and the irony is part of the argument. Poetic shorthand is always flagged when it touches formal reasoning.

original.text: 1. The Problem of Inner Recursion
original.name: The Problem of Inner Recursion

everyone.text: 1. The Problem of Inner Recursion
everyone.name: The Problem of Inner Recursion

original.text: Science is an inner-recursive enterprise: theories are constructed, validated, and revised using the very tools and standards they produce. This reflexivity is not merely sociological; it is structural. Any formal system capable of representing arithmetic is subject to Gödel-style limitations; any scientific framework capable of describing its own observation infrastructure faces an analogous incompleteness. By "inner recursion" I mean the inevitability that our explanatory apparatuses are defined from within the system they aim to describe, and therefore cannot exhaustively capture what lies outside the system's axioms.

everyone.text: **The technical text just said:** science builds its tools with its own theories, checks those theories with those tools, and revises them — from the inside. That reflexivity is structural, not merely sociological: any formal system strong enough to represent arithmetic hits Gödel-style limits, and any scientific framework strong enough to describe its own observation infrastructure hits an analogous wall. By "inner recursion" it means: our explanatory apparatuses are defined from *within* the system they are trying to explain — so they can never exhaustively capture what lies outside the system's own axioms. **Why that matters:** this is the engine of the whole paper. Science is a loop — and there is nothing wrong with a loop; it works brilliantly. The problem starts when a theory claims to describe **everything**, because the loop is by definition inside the sandbox, and the sandbox wall is invisible from inside. You can't see your own eye with your own eye.

original.text: We can only measure what we already know how to measure. Operational science measures what it can operationalize; what lies outside its parameterization is methodologically invisible — not refuted, not resolved, simply unregistered. A closed theory cannot natively register what it does not already encode. A genuine **TOE** would therefore need to account for itself, the unknown, and everything in between — all of reality — from inside a system that has, by construction, no way to represent what it does not already define. The problem is not that we lack the data; it is that "everything" is not a data-shaped object.

everyone.text: **Which said:** theory makes methods, methods make data, data makes theory — round and round, forever, all inside. And the consequence lands immediately: **we can only measure what we already know how to measure.** Whatever our tools cannot reach is not refuted and not resolved — it is simply unregistered; it does not exist in the paperwork. A closed theory cannot natively record what it does not already encode, which is why a genuine TOE would need to account for itself, the unknown, and everything in between, from inside a system that has, by construction, no way to represent what it does not already define. The problem is not that we lack data. It is that "everything" is not data-shaped. **And one more proof of the recursion, hiding in the spelling:** the phrase "Theory of Everything" is physically inside the word THEORY — **T-H-...TOE...-RY**. Every theory already contains its own theory-of-everything, quietly. That is the most compact demonstration of inner recursion you will ever find — the theory contains the theory, and neither can see past its own spelling. (Note on the acronym, for everyone's sanity: toes shall henceforth be referred to as "fingers.")

original.text: This is where scientific TOEs predictably fracture. To capture the unknown, one must extend the grammar of the known. But the moment a framework introduces new primitives to reach beyond its own closure, it outruns the evaluative procedures that conferred its credibility. The result is a category error in peer review: frameworks are penalized not for incoherence but for refusing to pretend that the boundary of method is the boundary of being. Hence the preponderance of "theories of most things."

everyone.text: **And then came the crack:** to capture the unknown, you must extend the grammar of the known — new words, new rules, new kinds of measurement. But the moment you do, the old procedures of proof can no longer judge you; so instead of being examined fairly, you get dismissed for leaving the building. The verdict handed down is not "wrong" but "not in our territory" — a category error in peer review: frameworks are penalized not for incoherence but for refusing to pretend that the boundary of method is the boundary of being. Enough of that, and the literature fills with its favorite product: not theories of everything, but **theories of most things**, stacked in a corner, each with a politely different label.

original.text: 4. Science, Religion, and the Measurement of Ultimacy
original.name: Science, Religion, and the Measurement of Ultimacy

everyone.text: 4. Science, Religion, and the Measurement of Ultimacy
everyone.name: Science, Religion, and the Measurement of Ultimacy

original.text: Both scientific and religious totalities are, in effect, self-defining systems. Religious accounts posit an ultimate reality — a creator, an origin — that serves as their identity operator; scientific TOEs attempt to enclose ultimate structure within empirical terms and formal laws. Religious frameworks declare their boundary conditions axiomatically; science infers boundaries empirically. Neither approach escapes the fundamental problem: if the ultimate operator that explains everything is not expressible within the same formalism, it remains experimentally and critically inaccessible to that formalism.

Religion declares its boundary conditions up front, as axioms; science infers its boundaries from evidence. Neither escapes the fundamental problem: **if the ultimate operator that explains everything is not expressible within the same formalism, it stays experimentally and critically inaccessible to that formalism.** Two closed rooms, each with its own front door — science says "show me," religion says "trust me," and each decides, from the inside, what counts as a good answer.

original.text: The symmetry runs deeper than method. Religion is a measurement of people's relationship to the ultimate; science is a measurement of ultimate reality itself. Both define their own admissible evidence, and both are self-contained — each excludes what lies beyond its own definitions: human experience for science, physical mechanism for religion. Neither, as ordinarily practiced, can transparently adjudicate what falls outside its own scope without altering its rules.

original.text: The stakes justify the detour: a TOE is, by definition, about everything, and everything includes the human relationship to totality. Any candidate that must bracket half of its subject matter in order to remain "scientific" has already conceded the argument. A meta-reality is required that contains both domains and the operation holding them together — in religious terms this operator has been called God; in formal terms it is the identity operator of section 2. Science struggles to explain the fullness of human experience; religion is often inadequate at describing the physical environment in which humans exist. A genuine TOE must allow for everything, and therefore cannot be confined to either.

original.text: 5. Consequences for Consciousness, Time, and Gravitation
original.name: Consequences for Consciousness, Time, and Gravitation

everyone.text: 5. Consequences for Consciousness, Time, and Gravitation
everyone.name: Consequences for Consciousness, Time, and Gravitation

original.text: The persistent recalcitrance of consciousness, the arrow of time, and gravity to seamless theoretical unification is not merely a technical gap; it is symptomatic of the deeper epistemic constraint described above. These phenomena are boundary phenomena — domains where the explanatory apparatus encounters its own limits. Consciousness is the apparatus experiencing itself; time is the frame in which measurement happens; gravity is the geometry of the arena in which the measuring instruments live. Each is entangled with the very conditions of explanation and measurement, which is why they refuse to behave like ordinary objects of inquiry. The difficulty is not merely discovering better equations; it is recognizing the domains where methodological extension is required.

everyone.text: **Which said:** $H$ is the class of human knowers; $\Omega$ is the totality of everything that is the case; and the formula reads: every individual human is finite, so no individual human can complete the infinite totality. End of story — the mathematical version of "one person cannot carry the ocean in a teacup." There is, presumably, such a totality — but it is not for us to know; we lack the capacity, the scale, and the time. An honest totalizing theory must therefore learn to live with the remainder it cannot absorb; that remainder is not an engineering problem but a structural fact. But watch the word *person* — the formula says *one* person. It says nothing about every-one. Because while a single one is finite... **everyone is the sum of the ones.** That is not metaphor; it is arithmetic: $\sum_{i=1}^{n} 1 = \text{everyone}$. Every one of us is a single "1"; all of us, added up, are the only instrument big enough to hold something infinite. That is the seed of the **Unified Theory of Everyone**, and it has a thought experiment attached: imagine one single person who is the living average of every person alive — a language made of the most-spoken words, a deliberately neutral accent, topics everyone actually cares about (birth, food, weather, work, love, death), expressions stripped of idioms. No single person can be that voice. But a theory built by everyone can — and every field that studies everyone (anthropology, sociology, statistics, linguistics with its born-anywhere creoles, globalization itself) is, without knowing it, a chapter of that book.

original.text: This diagnosis does not render scientific practice useless. Rather, it clarifies what a responsible pursuit of "more-everything" must acknowledge:

original.text:
- **Widen the aperture.** The exponential growth of scientific progress, data, and accessible knowledge generates a correspondingly exponential responsibility for everything and everyone outside science. Narrow, insular methodologies are no longer defensible; the discipline must expand its empirical and conceptual scope.
- **Make the meta-assumptions explicit.** Identify and formalize the identity-type operators and boundary conditions that current models tacitly assume — instead of discovering them after the fact, in the shape of anomalies.
- **Accept a non-empirical arena of structured inquiry.** Some aspects of a TOE will require novel conceptual tools and standards of critique not reducible to conventional peer-review metrics — without abandoning empirical rigor.
- **Address reductionism and the nature of explanation.** Without confronting how levels relate and how emergence constrains derivation, any TOE purchases neatness at the cost of relevance; it becomes, at best, a "theory of most things."

- **Widen the aperture.** Knowledge, data, and accessible progress grow exponentially — and so does the responsibility to everything and everyone outside science. Narrow, insular methodologies are no longer defensible; the discipline must expand its empirical and conceptual scope.
- **Make the meta-assumptions explicit.** Every model quietly assumes its own boundary conditions and identity-type operators. Write them on the tin: confess what you assumed, up front, like the fine print it is — instead of discovering it later, in the shape of anomalies.
- **Accept a non-empirical arena of structured inquiry.** Some aspects of a TOE will require novel conceptual tools and standards of critique not reducible to conventional peer-review metrics — without abandoning empirical rigor. That does not make it nonsense; it makes it *new*, deserving honest critique, not the silent treatment.
- **Address reductionism and the nature of explanation.** Without confronting how levels relate and how emergence constrains derivation, any TOE purchases neatness at the cost of relevance; it becomes, at best, a "theory of most things." Taking things apart teaches you the parts; it does not teach you the whole.

original.text: None of this will conjure omniscience. It is a proposal for a more honest discipline, not a shortcut to totality.

everyone.text: **And then the honesty clause:** none of this will conjure omniscience. It is a proposal for a more honest discipline, not a shortcut to totality. Which brings us to the modest proposal that gives this edition its name: **build the theory with everyone.** Every one of us is one; the Unified Theory of Everyone is simply the sum of everyone's ones — every field, every language, every way of knowing, every person who ever looked at the sky and wondered. Not a flattening into sameness: a genuine sum keeps every term. Unity without erasing the differences is the only kind of unity that survives contact with everyone — and it also happens to be the only kind that is *checkable*, because every one of us gets to read it, and if it is wrong about anyone, someone will say so. That, by the way, is the strongest peer-review mechanism that exists, hiding in plain sight.

original.text: 7. Conclusion — A Dark Irony
original.name: Conclusion — A Dark Irony

everyone.text: 7. Conclusion — A Dark Irony
everyone.name: Conclusion — A Dark Irony

original.text: A Theory of Everything is, by necessity, caught in a snake-eating-its-tail paradox: to be truly complete it must account for its own possibility — and once that possibility is fully known, the predicate "to know" loses the boundary that makes knowledge meaningful. Total comprehension collapses the contrast that makes knowing possible. A total absence of unknowns erases meaning itself.

original.text: Thus the most honest conclusion is ironically modest. There is an ultimate totality — an ultimate reality, an operator — but its full articulation is likely not attainable by agents constrained by the very structures that make articulation possible. A theory of everything is, in the end, a theory of every nothing: a theory of every unknown thing. Science remains our best instrument for mapping reality; it simply cannot be the sole apparatus for mapping the mapmaker.

And here is the punchline that makes the whole joke worth telling: **TOE was hiding inside THEORY the entire time** — and everyone is the sum of the ones. The Unified Theory of Everyone was never going to be finished by one genius up on a mountain; it was always going to be finished by every one of us, at kitchen tables, out loud, together. Congratulations: you've just started.

original.text: This is not defeatism but a challenge: to cultivate a scientific humility that admits where formalism must be extended, and a methodological courage that integrates meta-ontological reflection without abandoning empirical rigor. The strange, dark consolation is that the impossibility of absolute totalization preserves the domain of inquiry — and with it, the meaning of discovery.
